title: Algorithms
overview: Topic 9.2 is about designing an algorithm and writing it down precisely before it is programmed. It covers choosing identifiers and recording them in an identifier table; writing pseudocode with input, processing and output; the three basic constructs of sequence, selection and iteration; documenting an algorithm as structured English, a flowchart or pseudocode, and converting between those forms; logic statements that define conditions; and stepwise refinement, which breaks an outline into steps detailed enough to code. Paper 2 marks depend on correct Cambridge pseudocode keywords, sensible identifiers and logic that works for every input, so each example here is dry-run with a trace table.
syllabusPoints: Show understanding that an algorithm is a solution to a problem expressed as a sequence of defined steps.
Use suitable identifier names for the representation of data used by a problem and represent these using an identifier table.
Write pseudocode that contains input, process and output.
Write pseudocode using the three basic constructs of sequence, selection and iteration (repetition).
Document a simple algorithm using a structured English description, a flowchart or pseudocode.
Write pseudocode from a structured English description and from a flowchart.
Draw a flowchart from a structured English description and from pseudocode.
Describe and use the process of stepwise refinement to express an algorithm to a level of detail from which the task may be programmed.
Use logic statements to define parts of an algorithm solution.

definitions.definition: A solution to a problem written as a finite sequence of defined, unambiguous steps carried out in a set order.
The name given to a variable, constant, array or module so that it can be referred to in an algorithm.
A table listing each identifier used in a solution with its data type and an explanation of what it stores or does.
A restricted form of English made of short command statements (INPUT, SET, IF, REPEAT, OUTPUT) used to describe the steps of an algorithm.
A notation that uses keywords and identifiers to describe an algorithm like program code but without the syntax of any one programming language.
A diagram of an algorithm made of standard shapes (terminator, process, input/output, decision) joined by flow lines showing the order of steps.
The three basic constructs: steps run one after another; a condition chooses which steps run; a group of steps is repeated.
A condition built from relational operators (=, <>, <, >, <=, >=) and logical operators (AND, OR, NOT) that evaluates to TRUE or FALSE.
A value of the correct data type but outside the normal range, used only to mark the end of a sequence of inputs (e.g. -1 for marks).
Repeatedly breaking each step of an outline solution into smaller, more detailed steps until every step can be written directly as program code.

sections.title: What an algorithm is
content: An algorithm is a solution to a problem written as a sequence of defined steps. 'Defined' is the key word: each step must be exact, so anyone (or any computer) following it does the same thing and gets the same result. A good algorithm finishes after a finite number of steps for every valid input, and its steps are carried out in a fixed order.

Everyday instructions are algorithms too. Withdrawing cash at an ATM is: insert card; enter PIN; if the PIN is wrong, allow another try, up to three; choose an amount; if the balance is high enough, dispense the cash, otherwise show a message; return the card. Swap two of those steps, such as dispensing cash before checking the balance, and the process fails. The same instructions also show the three building blocks every algorithm uses: steps in order, choices and repetition.

Most computer algorithms take data in, process it and output a result. A problem can often be solved by several different algorithms; a better one gives correct results, is easy to follow, and uses less time and memory.
bullets: Every step must be unambiguous: 'add a bit of tax' is not a defined step; 'Tax ← Price * 0.2' is.
Order matters: the same steps in a different sequence can give a different or no result.
An algorithm is language-independent; it is designed first and then coded in any programming language.

sections.title: Documenting an algorithm: structured English, flowcharts and pseudocode
content: The syllabus names three ways to document an algorithm. Structured English uses a small set of English command words, such as INPUT, SET, IF, REPEAT, OUTPUT, written as short numbered or indented statements. It is quick to write and easy for a non-programmer to read, but it is not precise enough to code from without further work.

A flowchart draws the algorithm as a set of standard shapes joined by arrows. It makes the paths through selections and loops easy to see at a glance, but becomes hard to follow for long algorithms. Pseudocode uses the keywords and layout of the Cambridge pseudocode guide (DECLARE, ←, IF … THEN … ELSE … ENDIF, FOR … NEXT and so on) and is the closest of the three to real program code. A flowchart and its pseudocode should contain the same level of detail.
bullets: In pseudocode, ← means assignment and = means 'is equal to' in a condition; never swap them.
Indent the body of every IF, CASE and loop so that its extent is clear.
Every decision diamond needs exactly two labelled exits (Yes/No or TRUE/FALSE).
Flowcharts in exams are drawn with shapes; in these notes they are shown in a text form using the key below.

examples.label: Flowchart symbols and the text form used in these notes
examples.content:
Symbol (shape)                 | Used for                         | Text form used in these notes
Terminator (rounded / oval)    | START and END of the algorithm   | ( START )
Process (rectangle)            | assignment or calculation        | [ Total ← Total + Mark ]
Input/output (parallelogram)   | INPUT and OUTPUT                 | / INPUT Mark /
Decision (diamond)             | a condition with two exits       | < Mark > 50 ? >  with Yes / No labels
Subroutine (rectangle with     | CALL to a procedure              | [[ CALL PrintReport ]]
  double side lines)           |                                  |
Flow line (arrow)              | order of execution; a line that  | |  v  -->
                               | goes back up forms a loop        |

sections.title: The three basic constructs: sequence, selection, iteration
content: Any algorithm can be built from three constructs. Sequence means statements are executed one after another in the order written. Selection means a condition is tested and the result decides which group of statements runs; in pseudocode it is written with IF … THEN … ELSE … ENDIF for one or two choices, or CASE OF … OTHERWISE … ENDCASE when one value is compared with several options. Iteration (repetition) means a group of statements is executed more than once, using a FOR, REPEAT or WHILE loop.

Assignment, giving a variable a value with ←, is the basic statement placed inside these constructs; the coursebook lists it as a fourth construct. Input and output statements let the algorithm receive data and report results. Constructs can be nested: a selection inside a loop, a loop inside a selection, or one IF inside another (a nested IF).
bullets: Sequence: order of steps; selection: choose a path; iteration: repeat a block.
CASE is tidier than a long chain of nested IFs when one variable is tested against many values or ranges.
The same construct can be written in all three notations; the comparison table shows how.

examples.label: The three constructs in Cambridge pseudocode
examples.content:
// sequence
INPUT Width
INPUT Height
Area ← Width * Height

// selection: IF
IF Area > 100
   THEN
      OUTPUT "Large"
   ELSE
      OUTPUT "Small"
ENDIF

// selection: CASE
CASE OF Direction
   "N" : OUTPUT "North"
   "S" : OUTPUT "South"
   OTHERWISE : OUTPUT "Unknown"
ENDCASE

// iteration
FOR Row ← 1 TO 3
   OUTPUT Row
NEXT Row

sections.title: Pseudocode with input, process and output
content: Most algorithms follow the pattern input → process → output. Inputs are the data supplied from outside, typed by a user, read from a file or taken from a sensor, and are written with INPUT. Processing is everything done to the data: calculations, comparisons, validation, counting and totalling. Outputs are the results displayed or stored, written with OUTPUT; several items can be output in one statement separated by commas.

Before writing pseudocode it helps to list the three parts separately. Every input should be used by some process, and every output should be produced by one; if not, something is missing. The worked example below reads marks until a rogue value is entered, rejects any out of range, and outputs how many were valid and their mean.
bullets: Initialise totals and counters (usually to 0) before a loop that adds to them.
Guard against division by zero when an average could be taken of no values.
Choose a rogue value that can never be a genuine input; here -1, because marks are 0 to 100.

examples.label: Input, process and output for the class marks problem
examples.content:
Input   | Mark, entered repeatedly; -1 ends the input (rogue value)
Process | reject a mark outside 0 to 100; add each valid mark to Total and add 1 to Count;
        | after the loop, Average ← Total / Count
Output  | a message for each rejected mark; the number of valid marks and their average,
        | or a message if no valid marks were entered

examples.label: Pseudocode: average of valid marks
examples.content:
DECLARE Mark : INTEGER
DECLARE Total : INTEGER
DECLARE Count : INTEGER
DECLARE Average : REAL
Total ← 0
Count ← 0
INPUT Mark
WHILE Mark <> -1
   IF Mark >= 0 AND Mark <= 100
      THEN
         Total ← Total + Mark
         Count ← Count + 1
      ELSE
         OUTPUT "Mark rejected: ", Mark
   ENDIF
   INPUT Mark
ENDWHILE
IF Count > 0
   THEN
      Average ← Total / Count
      OUTPUT Count, " marks, average ", Average
   ELSE
      OUTPUT "No valid marks"
ENDIF

examples.label: Trace table: inputs 64, 105, 80, -1
examples.content:
Mark | Total | Count | Average | OUTPUT
     | 0     | 0     |         |
64   | 64    | 1     |         |
105  |       |       |         | Mark rejected: 105
80   | 144   | 2     |         |
-1   |       |       | 72      | 2 marks, average 72

-1 makes the WHILE condition FALSE, so the loop ends; 144 / 2 = 72. If -1 were the first input, the loop body would never run and "No valid marks" would be output.

sections.title: Identifiers, identifier tables and assignment
content: A variable is a named memory location holding a value that can change; its name is its identifier. Good identifiers describe their contents, such as NumberOfGuesses or TotalCost rather than N or X, which makes an algorithm self-documenting. The pseudocode guide's rules: an identifier starts with a letter and contains only letters, digits and the underscore, with no spaces; keywords such as INPUT or ENDIF cannot be used; and identifiers should be treated as case-insensitive, so never use two names that differ only in capital letters. Joining words with capitals (CamelCase) keeps long names readable.

An identifier table lists every identifier a solution needs, with its data type and a short explanation. Building it before writing pseudocode forces you to decide what data the problem really involves, and exam questions often ask for one.

Assignment uses ←: the expression on the right is evaluated and the result stored in the variable on the left. Count ← Count + 1 updates a variable using its own old value. Copying (B ← A) leaves A unchanged. Swapping two variables needs a third, temporary variable; otherwise the first copy overwrites a value that is still needed.
bullets: Explain each identifier's purpose, not just its type: 'Count: number of valid marks entered so far'.
Use constants for fixed values, e.g. CONSTANT VATRate ← 0.2, so the value is changed in one place.
Declare variables with DECLARE <identifier> : <data type> (INTEGER, REAL, CHAR, STRING, BOOLEAN, DATE).

examples.label: Identifier table for the class marks problem (section above)
examples.content:
Identifier | Data type | Explanation
Mark       | INTEGER   | the mark just input; -1 ends the input
Total      | INTEGER   | running total of the valid marks
Count      | INTEGER   | how many valid marks have been input
Average    | REAL      | Total / Count, calculated after the loop

examples.label: Swapping two values with a temporary variable
examples.content:
Pseudocode:            Trace (Left = 8, Right = 3 at the start):
Temp ← Left            Left | Right | Temp
Left ← Right           8    | 3     |
Right ← Temp                |       | 8
                       3    |       |
                            | 8     |

Result: Left = 3, Right = 8. Without Temp, Left ← Right followed by Right ← Left would leave both variables holding 3.

sections.title: Logic statements and selection
content: A logic statement is a condition that is either TRUE or FALSE. Simple conditions compare two values with a relational operator: = equal to, <> not equal to, <, >, <= and >=. More complex conditions combine simple ones with the logical operators AND (both must be true), OR (at least one must be true) and NOT (reverses the result); brackets make the order of evaluation clear.

Writing the rules of a problem as logic statements first is a reliable way to define the selection part of an algorithm. Each statement then becomes a branch of an IF or CASE. Check that the statements cover every possible value exactly once and pay special attention to the boundaries.
bullets: 'Between 5 and 15 inclusive' is Age >= 5 AND Age <= 15; a range can never be written 5 <= Age <= 15 in pseudocode.
In a nested IF, earlier conditions have already filtered values, so later tests can be simpler (Age <= 15 in the ELSE branch of Age < 5).
CASE ranges are written 5 TO 15 : and OTHERWISE catches anything not listed.
Test data should include each boundary value and the values either side of it.

examples.label: Logic statements for a cinema ticket price
examples.content:
Age < 5                   → Price is 0
Age >= 5 AND Age <= 15    → Price is 4
Age >= 16 AND Age <= 64   → Price is 9
Age >= 65                 → Price is 5
Each whole-number age satisfies exactly one statement.

examples.label: The same rules as nested IF and as CASE
examples.content:
INPUT Age
IF Age < 5
   THEN
      Price ← 0
   ELSE
      IF Age <= 15
         THEN
            Price ← 4
         ELSE
            IF Age <= 64
               THEN
                  Price ← 9
               ELSE
                  Price ← 5
            ENDIF
      ENDIF
ENDIF

// equivalent CASE (assumes Age has already been validated as >= 0)
CASE OF Age
   0 TO 4   : Price ← 0
   5 TO 15  : Price ← 4
   16 TO 64 : Price ← 9
   OTHERWISE : Price ← 5
ENDCASE
OUTPUT "Price: ", Price

examples.label: Boundary test table
examples.content:
Age | Branch taken            | Price
4   | Age < 5                 | 0
5   | Age <= 15               | 4
15  | Age <= 15               | 4
16  | Age <= 64               | 9
64  | Age <= 64               | 9
65  | final ELSE / OTHERWISE  | 5

sections.title: Iteration: FOR, REPEAT and WHILE loops
content: Pseudocode has three loops. A count-controlled loop, FOR Counter ← Start TO End … NEXT Counter, runs a known number of times; the counter goes up by 1 automatically, or by another amount with STEP. A post-condition loop, REPEAT … UNTIL condition, tests at the end, so its body always runs at least once, and it stops when the condition becomes TRUE. A pre-condition loop, WHILE condition … ENDWHILE, tests before each pass, so its body may run zero times, and it continues while the condition is TRUE.

Choose FOR when the number of repetitions is known before the loop starts; REPEAT when the body must run at least once, as in input validation or a password prompt; WHILE when the body might not need to run at all, as with a rogue value that could be the first input. Loops can be nested, with the inner loop completing all its passes for each pass of the outer loop.

A trace table is the standard way to check a loop by hand. It has a column for each variable and for output, and a new row each time values change. Dry-running with carefully chosen data shows whether the loop stops at the right point.
bullets: REPEAT … UNTIL stops when its condition is TRUE; WHILE continues while its condition is TRUE: the conditions are opposites.
Do not change the FOR counter inside the loop body.
Make sure something inside a REPEAT or WHILE loop can change the condition, or the loop never ends.
A combined condition such as UNTIL Correct OR Tries = 3 gives a loop two ways to stop.

examples.label: One example of each loop
examples.content:
// FOR: sum of the squares of 1 to 4
Total ← 0
FOR Index ← 1 TO 4
   Total ← Total + Index * Index
NEXT Index
OUTPUT Total

// REPEAT: up to three password attempts
Tries ← 0
REPEAT
   INPUT Attempt
   Tries ← Tries + 1
UNTIL Attempt = "Orange7" OR Tries = 3
IF Attempt = "Orange7"
   THEN
      OUTPUT "Access granted"
   ELSE
      OUTPUT "Locked"
ENDIF

// WHILE: years for 1000 to reach 2000 at 20% growth a year
Balance ← 1000
Years ← 0
WHILE Balance < 2000
   Balance ← Balance * 1.2
   Years ← Years + 1
ENDWHILE
OUTPUT Years

examples.label: Trace tables for the three loops
examples.content:
FOR loop                 REPEAT loop (inputs "apple", "Orange7")
Index | Total            Attempt   | Tries | OUTPUT
      | 0                          | 0     |
1     | 1                "apple"   | 1     |
2     | 5                "Orange7" | 2     | Access granted
3     | 14
4     | 30               With inputs "a", "b", "c" the loop stops
OUTPUT 30                because Tries = 3, and "Locked" is output.

WHILE loop
Balance | Years | Balance < 2000?
1000    | 0     | TRUE
1200    | 1     | TRUE
1440    | 2     | TRUE
1728    | 3     | TRUE
2073.6  | 4     | FALSE → loop ends, OUTPUT 4

examples.label: Why REPEAT suits counting digits
examples.content:
INPUT Number
Digits ← 0
REPEAT
   Number ← Number DIV 10
   Digits ← Digits + 1
UNTIL Number = 0
OUTPUT Digits

Number | Digits
4072   | 0
407    | 1
40     | 2
4      | 3
0      | 4      → OUTPUT 4

Written as WHILE Number > 0 instead, an input of 0 would skip the loop and output 0 digits; REPEAT guarantees one pass and correctly gives 1.

sections.title: Writing pseudocode from structured English and from a flowchart
content: To turn structured English into pseudocode, first build an identifier table from the nouns in the description (the data), then translate each statement into the matching construct: INPUT and OUTPUT stay as they are, calculations become assignments, 'if' becomes IF … ENDIF, and 'repeat' becomes whichever loop fits how the repetition ends. Add anything the English leaves implicit, such as setting a total to zero before the loop.

To turn a flowchart into pseudocode, follow the arrows from START. Parallelograms become INPUT or OUTPUT, rectangles become assignments and diamonds become conditions. A diamond whose arrow goes back up the chart is a loop: if the test comes before the body it is a WHILE loop; if the body comes first and the test is at the bottom it is a REPEAT … UNTIL loop. A diamond whose two paths rejoin further down is an IF.
bullets: Check the loop condition's direction: a flowchart that loops back on 'No' to 'Count = 9?' becomes UNTIL Count = 9.
Keep the flowchart's identifiers exactly; examiners check they are used consistently.
Dry-run the pseudocode with the same data as the flowchart to confirm they agree.

examples.label: From structured English: loyalty points
examples.content:
Structured English:
SET total points to zero
INPUT amount spent
WHILE amount is not zero
   CALCULATE points as the number of whole tens in the amount
   IF amount is 100 or more THEN DOUBLE the points
   ADD points to total points
   INPUT next amount
OUTPUT total points

Identifier table:
Identifier  | Data type | Explanation
Amount      | INTEGER   | amount spent on one purchase; 0 ends the input
Points      | INTEGER   | points for the current purchase
TotalPoints | INTEGER   | running total of points

examples.label: Pseudocode for the loyalty points description
examples.content:
DECLARE Amount : INTEGER
DECLARE Points : INTEGER
DECLARE TotalPoints : INTEGER
TotalPoints ← 0
INPUT Amount
WHILE Amount <> 0
   Points ← Amount DIV 10
   IF Amount >= 100
      THEN
         Points ← Points * 2
   ENDIF
   TotalPoints ← TotalPoints + Points
   INPUT Amount
ENDWHILE
OUTPUT "Points earned: ", TotalPoints

examples.label: Trace table: inputs 45, 120, 9, 0
examples.content:
Amount | Points | TotalPoints | OUTPUT
       |        | 0           |
45     | 4      | 4           |
120    | 24     | 28          |   (120 DIV 10 = 12, doubled)
9      | 0      | 28          |
0      |        |             | Points earned: 28

examples.label: From a flowchart: factorial of N
examples.content:
( START )
              |
         / INPUT N /
              |
      [ Result ← 1  ]
      [ Counter ← 1 ]
              |
   +--------->|
   |          v
   |   < Counter <= N ? > --No--> / OUTPUT Result / --> ( END )
   |          | Yes
   |  [ Result ← Result * Counter ]
   |  [ Counter ← Counter + 1     ]
   |          |
   +----------+

The test comes before the body and the arrow returns above it, so this is a pre-condition (WHILE) loop.

examples.label: Pseudocode written from the factorial flowchart
examples.content:
DECLARE N : INTEGER
DECLARE Result : INTEGER
DECLARE Counter : INTEGER
INPUT N
Result ← 1
Counter ← 1
WHILE Counter <= N
   Result ← Result * Counter
   Counter ← Counter + 1
ENDWHILE
OUTPUT Result

examples.label: Trace table: N = 4
examples.content:
N | Counter | Result | Counter <= N? | OUTPUT
4 | 1       | 1      | TRUE          |
  | 2       | 1      | TRUE          |
  | 3       | 2      | TRUE          |
  | 4       | 6      | TRUE          |
  | 5       | 24     | FALSE         | 24

4! = 1 × 2 × 3 × 4 = 24.

sections.title: Drawing a flowchart from structured English and from pseudocode
content: Drawing a flowchart is the reverse process: give each statement its standard shape and join them in execution order. Start and finish with terminators. Each INPUT or OUTPUT becomes a parallelogram and each assignment a rectangle. Each IF becomes a diamond whose Yes and No paths rejoin after the ENDIF. A CALL becomes a subroutine box.

Loops are drawn with a decision and an arrow going back. For WHILE, the diamond sits before the body and the 'continue' exit leads into the body. For REPEAT … UNTIL, the body comes first and the diamond sits after it, with the exit for 'condition FALSE' going back to the top of the body. For FOR, draw the counter being set, a diamond testing whether it has passed the end value, and a rectangle adding 1 at the end of the body.
bullets: Label both exits of every diamond.
One START and one END; every path must reach END.
Keep the same identifiers and conditions as the source so the two versions can be checked against each other.

examples.label: Flowchart from structured English: heater control
examples.content:
Structured English:
INPUT the room temperature
IF the temperature is below 18 THEN switch the heater on
OTHERWISE switch the heater off

              ( START )
                  |
            / INPUT Temp /
                  |
            < Temp < 18 ? >
           Yes |        | No
   [ Heater ← TRUE ]  [ Heater ← FALSE ]
               |        |
               +---+----+
                   |
                ( END )

Tests: Temp = 17 gives Heater TRUE; Temp = 18 gives Heater FALSE (18 is not below 18).

examples.label: Flowchart from pseudocode: the REPEAT password loop
examples.content:
( START )
                  |
           [ Tries ← 0 ]
                  |
   +------------->|
   |              v
   |       / INPUT Attempt /
   |              |
   |      [ Tries ← Tries + 1 ]
   |              |
   |  < Attempt = "Orange7" OR Tries = 3 ? >
   +------No------+
                  | Yes
        < Attempt = "Orange7" ? >
        Yes |              | No
 / OUTPUT "Access granted" /  / OUTPUT "Locked" /
            |              |
            +------+-------+
                   |
                ( END )

The body is drawn before the test, which is what makes this a post-condition loop.

sections.title: Stepwise refinement
content: Stepwise refinement takes an outline solution, a handful of broad steps, and repeatedly rewrites each step as a list of smaller, more exact steps. It stops when every step is a single input, output, assignment, selection or loop, so the result can be typed straight into a programming language. Numbering the levels (1, then 1.1, 1.2, then 1.2.1 …) shows which step each detail came from.

It is the algorithm-level version of decomposition from 9.1. Decomposition splits the problem into modules; stepwise refinement adds detail to the steps inside them. The refinements also reveal decisions the outline hid, such as how invalid input is handled or when a loop ends.
bullets: Refine one step at a time and keep the higher-level step as a comment, so the design remains readable.
A step is detailed enough when it maps to one pseudocode construct without further explanation.
Refinement often uncovers extra identifiers; add them to the identifier table as they appear.

examples.label: Refining 'grade a class and count the passes'
examples.content:
Level 1 (outline):
1 Set up: input the class size, set the pass count to 0
2 For each student: get a mark, grade it, output the grade, update the pass count
3 Output the number of passes

Level 2 (refining step 2):
2.1 Input a mark, repeating until it is between 0 and 100
2.2 Decide the grade: 70 or more is Distinction, 40 to 69 is Pass, below 40 is Fail
2.3 Output the student number and grade
2.4 If the mark is 40 or more, add 1 to the pass count

Level 3 (refining 2.1 and 2.2 into constructs):
2.1.1 REPEAT INPUT Mark UNTIL Mark >= 0 AND Mark <= 100
2.2.1 IF Mark >= 70 THEN Distinction
2.2.2 ELSE IF Mark >= 40 THEN Pass
2.2.3 ELSE Fail

examples.label: Final pseudocode after refinement
examples.content:
DECLARE ClassSize : INTEGER
DECLARE Student : INTEGER
DECLARE Mark : INTEGER
DECLARE Passes : INTEGER
DECLARE Grade : STRING
// 1 set up
Passes ← 0
INPUT ClassSize
// 2 each student
FOR Student ← 1 TO ClassSize
   REPEAT                                 // 2.1
      INPUT Mark
   UNTIL Mark >= 0 AND Mark <= 100
   IF Mark >= 70                          // 2.2
      THEN
         Grade ← "Distinction"
      ELSE
         IF Mark >= 40
            THEN
               Grade ← "Pass"
            ELSE
               Grade ← "Fail"
         ENDIF
   ENDIF
   OUTPUT Student, ": ", Grade             // 2.3
   IF Mark >= 40                          // 2.4
      THEN
         Passes ← Passes + 1
   ENDIF
NEXT Student
// 3 report
OUTPUT "Passes: ", Passes

examples.label: Trace table: ClassSize 3, marks 72, 150 (rejected), 45, 38
examples.content:
ClassSize | Student | Mark | Grade       | Passes | OUTPUT
3         |         |      |             | 0      |
          | 1       | 72   | Distinction | 1      | 1: Distinction
          | 2       | 150  |             |        |   (UNTIL is FALSE, input again)
          |         | 45   | Pass        | 2      | 2: Pass
          | 3       | 38   | Fail        | 2      | 3: Fail
          |         |      |             |        | Passes: 2

comparisonTable.title: The same constructs in structured English, pseudocode and a flowchart
rows: Assignment / sequence
SET Total TO 0, then ADD Mark TO Total
Total ← 0 then Total ← Total + Mark
Rectangles joined top to bottom by arrows
Input / output
INPUT the mark; OUTPUT the average
INPUT Mark / OUTPUT "Average: ", Average
Parallelogram
Selection
IF the mark is 40 or more THEN … OTHERWISE …
IF Mark >= 40 THEN … ELSE … ENDIF, or CASE OF … OTHERWISE … ENDCASE
Diamond with labelled Yes/No exits that rejoin
Iteration
REPEAT … UNTIL the mark is valid; WHILE there are marks left …
FOR … TO … NEXT, REPEAT … UNTIL, WHILE … ENDWHILE
Diamond with an arrow looping back to an earlier step
Strength
Quick to write, readable by non-programmers
Precise and closest to program code
Shows branches and loops visually
Weakness
Can be ambiguous; not detailed enough to code from
Must follow the syntax conventions
Hard to draw and follow for long algorithms

diagram.title: From problem statement to a programmable algorithm
nodes: Write an outline in structured English
Express it in pseudocode or a flowchart using sequence, selection and iteration
Dry-run with a trace table, including boundary and rogue values

analysisChains.title: Choosing the right loop for input validation
steps: A mark must be input and re-input until it lies between 0 and 100
The input must happen at least once, whatever the value
A REPEAT … UNTIL loop runs its body before testing, so it always asks at least once
The condition is written as the valid state: UNTIL Mark >= 0 AND Mark <= 100
analysisChains.evaluation: Matching the loop to how the repetition behaves avoids duplicated INPUT statements; a WHILE version would need an INPUT before the loop and another inside it, with the opposite condition.

analysisChains.title: Turning rules into logic statements before coding
steps: A problem states four ticket prices for age bands
Each band is written as a logic statement with explicit boundaries using AND
The statements are checked to cover every age exactly once
They are converted into a nested IF or a CASE with ranges, then tested at 4, 5, 15, 16, 64 and 65
analysisChains.evaluation: Defining the conditions as logic statements first exposes gaps and overlaps before any code is written, and tells you exactly which boundary values to test.

analysisChains.title: Why stepwise refinement produces programmable detail
steps: The outline says 'grade each student', which cannot be coded directly
Refinement splits it into input with validation, deciding the grade, output and counting
Each sub-step is refined again until it is one construct, such as a REPEAT or a nested IF
The final pseudocode maps line for line onto program code
analysisChains.evaluation: Refinement turns a vague outline into exact steps and brings hidden decisions to the surface, such as how invalid marks are handled, which would otherwise surface as bugs during coding.

examTips: Use ← for assignment and = only in conditions; close every block with its matching keyword (ENDIF, ENDCASE, NEXT <counter>, UNTIL, ENDWHILE).
When asked for an identifier table, give a meaningful identifier, a data type and a clear explanation for every variable the algorithm uses.
When converting a flowchart, check where the decision sits relative to the loop body: test first means WHILE, test last means REPEAT … UNTIL; UNTIL takes the opposite condition to WHILE.
Initialise totals and counters before loops, and output results after the loop unless the question asks for output on every pass.
Dry-run your own answer with a boundary value and a rogue value before moving on: it is the quickest way to catch an off-by-one or never-ending loop.
commonMistakes: Writing a range as 5 <= Age <= 15 instead of Age >= 5 AND Age <= 15.
Using = for assignment, or writing Count + 1 on its own line without assigning it back to Count.
Reversing a loop condition when converting between WHILE and REPEAT … UNTIL.
Forgetting to initialise a running total, or resetting it inside the loop so it never accumulates.
Processing the rogue value as data, for example adding -1 into the total before the loop checks for it.
Drawing a decision diamond with unlabelled exits, or a flowchart path that never reaches END.

quickRecall.question: What is an algorithm?
quickRecall.answer: A finite set of exact steps, carried out in a fixed order, that solves a problem.

quickRecall.question: What three things does an identifier table record?
quickRecall.answer: Each identifier's name, its data type and an explanation of what it stores or does.

quickRecall.question: Which loop always runs its body at least once?
When should you use a FOR loop?
quickRecall.answer: When the number of repetitions is known before the loop starts.

quickRecall.question: How is 'between 13 and 19 inclusive' written as a logic statement?
What is a rogue value?
quickRecall.answer: A value of the right data type but outside the normal range, used only to mark the end of input, such as -1 for marks.

quickRecall.question: What is stepwise refinement?
quickRecall.answer: Repeatedly breaking each step of an outline solution into smaller steps until each can be programmed directly.
